title: Object Detection Using Quantum Transfer Learning
authors: Mohammad Bahrami, Morteza Rafiee, Mohsen Norouzi
abstract: Object detection requires the joint learning of semantic identity and continuous spatial geometry. Existing quantum transfer learning approaches have focused mainly on classification tasks and do not support regression. Here, we introduce a physics informed hybrid classical-quantum architecture for object detection in which a pre-trained MobileNetV2 maps visual features into an eight qubits variationally quantum Hilbert space. The Hilbert space is partitioned into two task specific subspaces for semantic classification and geometric localization. Local quantum expectation values are used to predict continuous bounding box coordinates, while circuit topology regulates the flow of quantum information between the two tasks. We compare linear and circular CNOT topologies and show that periodic boundary conditions suppress bipartite entanglement without degrading detection performance. The circular architecture reaches a bipartite von Neumann entropy of 0.1688 bits and a Meyer-Wallach entanglement measure of 0.0370, while achieving an mAP@0.5 of 0.9448 and an mAP@0.5:0.95 of 0.6558. A thermodynamic formulation further interprets the total learning loss as a variation in Helmholtz free energy. It interprets geometric localization as an effective internal energy contribution and semantic classification as an entropic contribution. These results indicate that high performance in the proposed object detection model does not require maximal entanglement. Instead, efficient learning can emerge through topology controlled information flow, targeted restriction of entanglement, and information renormalization within the Hilbert space.
summary: This paper proposes a novel hybrid classical-quantum architecture for object detection, extending quantum transfer learning beyond simple classification. By formulating the learning process using a thermodynamic lens, the authors show that controlled information flow and targeted entanglement restriction, rather than maximal entanglement, are sufficient for achieving state-of-the-art performance while drastically reducing model complexity.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of performing object detection, which requires jointly learning semantic identity (classification) and continuous spatial geometry (regression), a task poorly supported by existing quantum transfer learning methods.
main_result: The proposed hybrid model achieves high object detection performance comparable to classical baselines while significantly reducing trainable parameters, demonstrating that efficient learning relies on topology-controlled information flow rather than maximal entanglement.
method: It introduces a physics-informed hybrid classical-quantum architecture where visual features are mapped into a variational quantum Hilbert space partitioned for the two tasks. The learning process is formulated using a thermodynamic analogy, interpreting the loss as a variation in Helmholtz free energy.
model_or_system: The system uses a pre-trained MobileNetV2 backbone to generate features, which are then encoded into an eight-qubit variational quantum circuit. The circuit's topology (linear vs. circular CNOT) regulates information flow between the semantic and geometric subspaces.
key_observables: mAP@0.5 (0.9448), mAP@0.5:0.95 (0.6558), bipartite von Neumann entropy (0.1688 bits for circular), and Meyer-Wallach entanglement measure (0.0370).
important_parameters: 10,366 trainable parameters (99.31% reduction vs. classical baseline); the structure of the quantum circuit topology (linear vs. circular).
main_assumptions: The classical backbone (MobileNetV2) is kept frozen, and the learning process can be effectively modeled by interpreting the total loss as a variation in Helmholtz free energy.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the architecture flow from MobileNetV2 through the Dressed Quantum Circuit (DQC) for object detection. Figure 6 shows visual detection results comparing the model's predictions to ground truth labels.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the gap in QTL for regression tasks. It then details the hybrid architecture, mapping features to a quantum state and partitioning the Hilbert space. The core contribution involves the thermodynamic formulation of the loss and comparing topological structures (linear vs. circular) to show that controlled entanglement is key to performance.
why_interesting: The thermodynamic interpretation of the learning loss (Helmholtz free energy) provides a deep physical framework for understanding the optimization landscape in quantum machine learning, linking information theory (entropy) directly to physical energy concepts.
